concepts.title: Cycles of the sky

date.label: c. 2000 BCE and earlier
date.note: Observational traditions developed independently over millennia; this is a broad placement, not an invention date.

concepts.summary: Repeated movements of the Sun, Moon, and stars made time and seasons observable patterns.
concepts.problem: Communities needed calendars, seasonal markers, and ways to orient travel.
concepts.development: Observers in Mesopotamia, Egypt, China, and other societies accumulated records. Later Maya astronomy and Polynesian navigation developed distinct, sophisticated uses of celestial regularities.
concepts.limitations: The surviving record is uneven; shared observations do not establish a single origin or direct transmission.

contributors.name: Anonymous observers
contributors.role: Maintained local calendrical and navigational traditions

concepts.title: Geocentric planetary models

date.label: c. 150 CE
date.note: Placement follows Ptolemy's Almagest; Earth-centered models are substantially older.

concepts.summary: Earth-centered mathematical models described planetary positions using combinations of circular motions.
concepts.problem: Planets sometimes appear to reverse direction against the stars.
concepts.development: Ptolemy synthesized earlier Greek mathematical astronomy into a predictive system. Later astronomers in multiple regions criticized and refined its geometry.
concepts.limitations: The model's stationary Earth is physically incorrect; its geometrical prediction techniques retain historical importance.

concepts.title: Heliocentric planetary system

date.note: Publication of De revolutionibus; earlier Sun-centered proposals existed.

concepts.summary: Placing Earth among the planets makes apparent planetary reversals a consequence of relative orbital motion.
concepts.problem: Astronomers sought a coherent arrangement of planetary periods and motions.
concepts.development: Copernicus reorganized inherited planetary geometry around the Sun. His circular-orbit construction was later revised through observations and Kepler's ellipses.
concepts.limitations: The Sun is not the center of the universe, and circular orbits were an approximation.

concepts.title: Kepler's laws of planetary motion

date.note: The first two laws appeared in 1609; the period–distance law followed in 1619.

concepts.summary: Planets follow ellipses, sweep equal areas in equal times, and obey a period–distance relation.
concepts.problem: Precise observations of Mars resisted circular-orbit models.
concepts.development: Kepler analyzed Tycho Brahe's positional measurements within a heliocentric framework. The resulting empirical rules helped make Newton's gravitational explanation possible.
concepts.limitations: The laws describe ideal two-body motion; interactions between planets require corrections.

equation.explanation: For bodies orbiting the same dominant mass, squared orbital period T is proportional to cubed semi-major axis a.

concepts.title: Stellar parallax

date.note: Bessel's published distance to 61 Cygni is used as the milestone; Struve and Henderson also contributed.

concepts.summary: A nearby star's apparent annual shift gives its distance through triangulation.
concepts.problem: Apparent brightness alone cannot tell a faint nearby star from a bright distant one.
concepts.development: Improved telescopes made tiny angular shifts measurable. Earth's orbit supplied the baseline, creating a geometric anchor for the cosmic distance ladder.
concepts.limitations: Parallax angles shrink with distance; measurement uncertainty eventually dominates.

equation.explanation: Distance d is in parsecs when annual parallax p is measured in arcseconds.

concepts.title: Stellar spectral classification

date.label: c. 1901
date.note: Marks Cannon's early classification work; the system developed across several decades.

concepts.summary: Patterns of absorption lines sort stars into classes closely related to surface temperature.
concepts.problem: Astronomers needed a consistent way to compare thousands of stellar spectra.
concepts.development: Williamina Fleming, Antonia Maury, and Annie Jump Cannon refined Harvard's classifications. Later atomic physics explained why temperature changes spectral lines.
concepts.limitations: A spectral class is not a complete history of a star; gravity, composition, and other properties also matter.

concepts.title: Cepheid period–luminosity relation

date.note: Leavitt identified the trend in 1908 and published its quantitative form in 1912.

concepts.summary: A Cepheid variable's pulsation period predicts its intrinsic brightness and therefore helps reveal its distance.
concepts.problem: Distances beyond the reach of parallax required another calibrated ruler.
concepts.development: Henrietta Swan Leavitt compared variables in the Magellanic Clouds, treating them as approximately equidistant. The relation became a bridge from nearby stars to other galaxies.
concepts.limitations: Different Cepheid populations and dust require calibration; the relation is not identical for every variable star.

contributors.name: Henrietta Swan Leavitt
contributors.role: Discovered the relation using photographic records

concepts.title: Hertzsprung–Russell diagram

date.label: c. 1911–1913
date.note: Independent early diagrams by Hertzsprung and Russell are represented by the 1913 milestone.

concepts.summary: Plotting stellar luminosity against temperature reveals the main sequence, giants, and white dwarfs.
concepts.problem: A catalog of stellar measurements needed an organizing pattern.
concepts.development: Hertzsprung and Russell connected spectral properties with intrinsic brightness. Stellar physics later explained how stars move through this diagram as they evolve.
concepts.limitations: A star's position alone does not uniquely determine its age, especially without mass and composition.

concepts.title: Expansion of the universe

date.note: Lemaître's theoretical and observational relation preceded Hubble's 1929 publication.

concepts.summary: On large scales, distances between unbound galaxies increase as the universe evolves.
concepts.problem: Galaxy spectra and distance estimates suggested a systematic pattern of recession.
concepts.development: Friedmann and Lemaître developed evolving relativistic models. Lemaître connected expansion with observations; Hubble's distances and Slipher's redshifts helped establish the empirical relation.
concepts.limitations: Bound systems do not simply expand with the universe; nearby peculiar velocities complicate the relation.

equation.explanation: For nearby galaxies in the large-scale flow, recession speed v is approximately the Hubble parameter H₀ times distance d.

concepts.title: Hot Big Bang cosmology

date.note: The placement marks Lemaître's early-origin proposal; the hot nuclear model developed in the 1940s.

concepts.summary: The observable universe evolved from a much hotter, denser early state as space expanded.
concepts.problem: Cosmology needed to explain expansion, light-element abundances, and the thermal history of matter.
concepts.development: Lemaître's early proposal was substantially revised by Gamow, Alpher, and Herman into a hot-universe framework. Background radiation later supplied strong observational evidence.
concepts.limitations: The model describes early evolution; it does not establish creation from absolute nothing or a complete account of the first instant.

contributors.name: Georges Lemaître
contributors.role: Proposed an early dense cosmic state

contributors.name: George Gamow, Ralph Alpher, and Robert Herman

concepts.title: Nuclear fusion in stars

date.note: Bethe's analysis of stellar energy production is the milestone; earlier contributions were essential.

concepts.summary: Stars release energy by transforming light nuclei into more tightly bound nuclei.
concepts.problem: Chemical burning and gravitational contraction could not explain the Sun's long lifetime.
concepts.development: Mass–energy equivalence and nuclear physics enabled proton–proton and carbon–nitrogen–oxygen reaction models. Bethe's work connected these reactions to stellar temperatures.
concepts.limitations: Reaction rates depend on temperature and composition; different masses follow different burning histories.

contributors.name: Arthur Eddington
contributors.role: Argued for nuclear energy in stars

concepts.title: Stellar nucleosynthesis

date.note: Marks the B2FH synthesis of element-production mechanisms, building on earlier stellar-nuclear work.

concepts.summary: Nuclear reactions in stars and stellar explosions build many elements heavier than helium.
concepts.problem: A physical explanation was needed for the observed distribution of chemical elements.
concepts.development: Burbidge, Burbidge, Fowler, and Hoyle organized distinct fusion and neutron-capture processes. Subsequent observations and calculations refined where those processes occur.
concepts.limitations: No single kind of star makes all elements; some production sites and detailed yields remain active research.

contributors.name: Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler, and Fred Hoyle

concepts.title: White dwarfs and the mass limit

date.note: Placement marks Chandrasekhar's relativistic mass-limit result; white dwarfs were observed earlier.

concepts.summary: Electron degeneracy pressure supports compact stellar remnants only below a limiting mass.
concepts.problem: Extremely dense, dim stars could not be explained as ordinary gas spheres.
concepts.development: Quantum statistics explained support without ongoing fusion. Chandrasekhar included relativistic electron motion and found a limiting mass near 1.4 solar masses.
concepts.limitations: The ideal limit depends on composition and assumptions; rotation, magnetic fields, and binary evolution add complications.

contributors.name: Ralph Fowler
contributors.role: Applied electron degeneracy to white dwarfs

concepts.title: Neutron stars and pulsars

date.note: Theory preceded the 1967 discovery of pulsars.

concepts.summary: A collapsed stellar core can form an object so dense that neutron-rich matter dominates its interior.
concepts.problem: Supernova remnants required a possible end state beyond ordinary stars and white dwarfs.
concepts.development: Baade and Zwicky proposed neutron stars after the neutron's discovery. Jocelyn Bell Burnell's pulsar observations later revealed rapidly rotating compact stars.
concepts.limitations: The behavior of matter at the highest core densities remains uncertain; not every neutron star is visible as a pulsar.

concepts.title: Black holes

date.label: 1916 onward
date.note: Schwarzschild's solution is the mathematical milestone; physical collapse and observational evidence came later.

concepts.summary: A black hole contains a region from which light cannot escape to distant observers.
concepts.problem: General relativity allowed gravity far stronger than Newtonian intuition suggested.
concepts.development: Schwarzschild found a spherical spacetime solution. Later collapse studies established physical formation scenarios; stellar orbits, accretion, and gravitational waves supplied evidence.
concepts.limitations: Classical singularities signal incomplete physics; the interior requires more than an extrapolation of tested external behavior.

contributors.name: J. Robert Oppenheimer and Hartland Snyder

concepts.title: Cosmic microwave background

date.note: Marks observational discovery; hot-universe radiation had been predicted earlier.

concepts.summary: A nearly uniform microwave glow preserves a cooled remnant of the universe's hot early phase.
concepts.problem: A hot Big Bang needed observable evidence beyond expansion.
concepts.development: Penzias and Wilson detected unexplained antenna noise. Dicke's group interpreted the radiation cosmologically; later satellites measured its spectrum and tiny anisotropies.
concepts.limitations: Foreground emission and instrumental calibration must be separated from the primordial signal.

concepts.title: Dark matter

date.label: 1933 onward
date.note: Zwicky's cluster analysis is a milestone; earlier missing-mass discussions existed.

concepts.summary: Multiple gravitational observations indicate more mass than luminous matter alone accounts for.
concepts.problem: Galaxy and cluster motions were too fast for the visible mass estimates.
concepts.development: Zwicky studied galaxy clusters; Rubin, Ford, and others extended evidence through galaxy rotation. Lensing and cosmology now provide independent constraints.
concepts.limitations: The gravitational discrepancy is well evidenced, but the identity of dark matter remains unresolved; alternatives must match multiple tests.

contributors.name: Fritz Zwicky
contributors.role: Inferred missing mass in the Coma cluster

concepts.title: Cosmic inflation

date.note: Guth's published proposal is the milestone; related ideas and subsequent models have distinct histories.

concepts.summary: A proposed brief period of accelerated early expansion could explain large-scale uniformity and seed cosmic structure.
concepts.problem: The basic hot-universe model leaves puzzles about flatness and causally separated regions.
concepts.development: Guth connected early-universe particle physics with rapid expansion. Linde and others developed models avoiding problems in the original scenario.
concepts.limitations: Some broad predictions fit observations, but no unique mechanism or inflation-driving field has been established.

concepts.title: Accelerated expansion and dark energy

date.note: Two independent supernova teams reported the key acceleration evidence.

concepts.summary: The late universe's expansion accelerates; dark energy names a component used to explain this within standard cosmology.
concepts.problem: Distant supernova distances did not fit a universe slowing under matter's gravity alone.
concepts.development: Teams compared standardized supernova brightness with redshift. Other cosmological measurements supported acceleration and constrained possible explanations.
concepts.limitations: Acceleration has strong evidence; whether its cause is a cosmological constant, a dynamical field, or modified gravity remains unresolved.

contributors.name: Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess's team

concepts.title: Planets beyond the Solar System

date.note: Pulsar planets were confirmed in 1992; a planet around a Sun-like star followed in 1995.

concepts.summary: Planets orbit other stars and remnants, revealing a much wider range of planetary systems than our own.
concepts.problem: Faint planets are difficult to distinguish beside bright host stars.
concepts.development: Wolszczan and Frail detected pulsar timing variations. Mayor and Queloz used stellar radial velocity; transit surveys later greatly expanded the sample.
concepts.limitations: Detection methods favor particular sizes and orbits; a catalog is not an unbiased census.

concepts.title: Gravitational deflection and lensing

date.note: The eclipse tests established a milestone in light deflection; observed strong lenses came later.

concepts.summary: Gravity bends light paths, allowing massive objects to distort, magnify, or multiply distant images.
concepts.problem: Relativity's prediction about light needed observational tests.
concepts.development: The 1919 eclipse expeditions measured stellar deflections. Later lensing observations turned this effect into a method for mapping mass and studying distant galaxies.
concepts.limitations: Mass reconstruction has degeneracies; the early eclipse data had substantial uncertainties and were followed by more precise tests.

contributors.name: Arthur Eddington, Frank Dyson, and expedition teams

concepts.title: Gravitational-wave astronomy

date.label: 2015 detection; 2016 announcement
date.note: The date follows the first direct detection, GW150914.

concepts.summary: Tiny changes in distance reveal passing spacetime waves from systems such as merging black holes.
concepts.problem: Many compact-object events are hard to study through light alone.
concepts.development: Relativity predicted the waves; laser interferometers and sophisticated noise analysis made direct detection possible. Observations opened a new way to test gravity.
concepts.limitations: Detectors cover limited frequency ranges and need careful calibration; source interpretation depends on waveform models.

contributors.name: LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration
contributors.role: Established direct detection and source interpretation

concepts.title: Radio astronomy

date.note: Jansky's published cosmic-radio discovery is the milestone.

concepts.summary: Radio receivers reveal celestial processes invisible to optical telescopes.
concepts.problem: Unexplained radio interference raised the possibility of emission from space.
concepts.development: Jansky traced a recurring signal to the Milky Way. Reber built a dedicated radio telescope; later arrays combined antennas to sharpen resolution.
concepts.limitations: Radio interference and Earth's atmosphere constrain observations; long wavelengths require large apertures or interferometers.

contributors.name: Grote Reber
contributors.role: Built an early dedicated radio telescope

concepts.title: The cosmic web

date.label: c. 1986
date.note: Marks a landmark redshift-survey map, not the first discovery of galaxy clustering.

concepts.summary: Galaxies form filaments, walls, clusters, and voids across enormous volumes.
concepts.problem: Two-dimensional sky positions concealed the three-dimensional organization of galaxies.
concepts.development: Redshift surveys supplied approximate depth information. The mapped structure became a test of gravitational growth from initial density fluctuations.
concepts.limitations: Galaxy surveys have selection effects, and redshift distances also contain local motion.

contributors.name: Margaret Geller, John Huchra, and Valérie de Lapparent
contributors.role: Mapped striking structure in the CfA redshift survey

concepts.title: Lambda–cold dark matter cosmology

date.label: c. 2003
date.note: WMAP's first-year results are a precision-era milestone; the model developed earlier.

concepts.summary: A compact cosmological model combines ordinary matter, cold dark matter, and a cosmological constant.
concepts.problem: Many observations of the early and late universe needed a consistent quantitative framework.
concepts.development: Background-radiation measurements, galaxy surveys, and supernova distances jointly constrained a small set of cosmological parameters.
concepts.limitations: Its components are partly phenomenological; the nature of dark matter and dark energy and several measurement tensions remain open.

contributors.name: WMAP and broader cosmology collaborations
contributors.role: Constrained the concordance model with multiple observations

concepts.title: Counting boards and the abacus

date.label: c. 500 BCE and earlier
date.note: A broad ancient milestone; different counting-board traditions have uncertain beginnings.

concepts.summary: Counters arranged by position make arithmetic visible and reduce demands on memory.
concepts.problem: Trade and administration required dependable calculations beyond mental arithmetic.
concepts.development: Ancient counting surfaces evolved into diverse bead and rod devices. Moving counters implemented numerical operations without requiring modern written notation.
concepts.limitations: No single inventor or uninterrupted transmission explains all abacus traditions; the device still relies on trained procedures.

concepts.title: Mechanical arithmetic

date.note: Pascal's calculator is the milestone, not a claim that it was the earliest calculating machine.

concepts.summary: Gear mechanisms can encode digits and automatically carry between numerical positions.
concepts.problem: Repeated bookkeeping arithmetic was laborious and prone to mistakes.
concepts.development: Pascal built adding devices; Leibniz later developed a stepped mechanism for more operations. Mechanical calculation made numerical procedures into engineered processes.
concepts.limitations: Early machines had restricted operations and manufacturing difficulties; programmable computation required additional ideas.

concepts.title: Programmable analytical engine

date.label: c. 1837
date.note: Babbage developed designs during the 1830s; Lovelace's published notes followed in 1843.

concepts.summary: A general-purpose calculating machine separates stored numbers, processing, and instructions.
concepts.problem: A machine built for one numerical table could not easily perform a different procedure.
concepts.development: Babbage extended his mechanical-engine ideas toward conditional, programmable calculation. Lovelace explained its broader symbolic possibilities and published a detailed computational example.
concepts.limitations: The complete engine was not built in their lifetimes; resemblance to later computers does not prove every later inventor drew directly from it.

contributors.name: Ada Lovelace
contributors.role: Explained its generality and published algorithmic notes

concepts.title: Turing machine

date.note: Turing's paper was published across 1936–1937.

concepts.summary: A finite rulebook, a movable head, and an unlimited tape provide a precise model of computation.
concepts.problem: Mathematicians needed a rigorous meaning for a calculation performed by mechanical rules.
concepts.development: Turing analyzed elementary symbolic steps and described a universal machine able to simulate other machines. This became a foundation for computability theory.
concepts.limitations: An unlimited tape is an idealization; computability does not guarantee practical running time.

concepts.title: Lambda calculus

date.label: 1930s; 1936 milestone
date.note: Church introduced the formalism earlier in the 1930s; 1936 marks its computability role.

concepts.summary: Computation can be expressed through defining functions and applying them to arguments.
concepts.problem: Logic needed precise rules for transforming expressions and representing effective procedures.
concepts.development: Church developed a calculus of function abstraction. Its correspondence with other computation models helped establish a robust notion of computability.
concepts.limitations: Untyped expressions may fail to terminate; typed variants impose additional restrictions.

contributors.name: Alonzo Church
contributors.role: Developed lambda calculus and its computability interpretation

concepts.example: The expression (λx. x + 1) applied to 4 evaluates to 5: define a rule, then supply its argument.

concepts.title: Limits of algorithmic decision

date.note: Turing's undecidability results underlie the modern halting-problem formulation.

concepts.summary: No single algorithm can correctly decide whether every possible program eventually stops.
concepts.problem: Could all mathematical and computational questions be settled by mechanical procedure?
concepts.development: Self-reference and a precise machine model produce a contradiction for any proposed universal stopping test. This sharply limits automatic reasoning.
concepts.limitations: Many restricted classes of programs can be analyzed; undecidability concerns an unrestricted universal procedure.

contributors.name: Alonzo Church
contributors.role: Independently proved a related undecidability result

concepts.title: Artificial neural networks

date.note: Marks the McCulloch–Pitts logical neuron model; trainable networks developed later.

concepts.summary: Networks of simple units transform inputs through connections, providing models for computation and learning.
concepts.problem: Could elementary neuron-like operations realize complex logical behavior?
concepts.development: McCulloch and Pitts related threshold units to propositional logic. Later learning rules made network weights adjustable from experience.
concepts.limitations: Artificial units simplify biological neurons drastically; their success does not by itself explain how brains work.

contributors.name: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts
contributors.role: Linked idealized neural activity with logic

concepts.title: Stored-program computing

date.note: The EDVAC draft appeared in 1945; working electronic implementations followed.

concepts.summary: Instructions encoded in memory can be changed and manipulated like other data.
concepts.problem: Rewiring a machine for every new computation limited flexibility.
concepts.development: EDVAC discussions and von Neumann's report articulated a stored-program design; teams in Manchester and Cambridge demonstrated practical machines.
concepts.limitations: Credit is collective and historically contested; a single architectural diagram does not capture all computer designs.

contributors.name: J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly

concepts.title: Mathematical information theory

date.note: Publication of Shannon's two-part mathematical theory of communication.

concepts.summary: Probability quantifies uncertainty, while coding theorems set limits on compression and reliable communication.
concepts.problem: Engineers needed to separate fundamental communication limits from particular devices.
concepts.development: Shannon modeled sources and noisy channels, deriving entropy and channel capacity. The theory linked statistics, coding, and communication engineering.
concepts.limitations: Shannon information measures uncertainty, not a message's truth, usefulness, or meaning.

contributors.name: Claude Shannon
contributors.role: Founded the mathematical theory of communication

equation.explanation: Entropy H is the average uncertainty, in bits, for possible outcomes x with probabilities p(x).

concepts.example: A fair yes/no event carries one bit of uncertainty. A nearly certain outcome carries less average uncertainty.

concepts.title: Cybernetics and feedback

date.note: Publication of Wiener's Cybernetics; feedback mechanisms themselves are much older.

concepts.summary: A system can regulate its behavior by measuring outputs and feeding that information back into its actions.
concepts.problem: Engineers and physiologists faced parallel problems of control under uncertainty.
concepts.development: Wiener connected communication, feedback, and statistical reasoning across machines and living systems. Control theory and cognitive models developed related approaches.
concepts.limitations: A shared feedback vocabulary does not make biological or social systems identical to simple machines.

concepts.title: Error-correcting codes

date.note: Publication of Hamming's coding paper.

concepts.summary: Carefully added redundancy allows some corrupted messages to be detected and repaired.
concepts.problem: Noisy channels and unreliable components can flip symbols during storage or transmission.
concepts.development: Hamming constructed codes with mathematical spacing between valid messages. Coding theory developed practical ways to approach communication limits.
concepts.limitations: Correction guarantees depend on the assumed error model and redundancy; arbitrary corruption cannot always be repaired.

contributors.name: Richard Hamming
contributors.role: Constructed influential error-detecting and correcting codes

concepts.title: Artificial intelligence as a research field

date.note: Dartmouth summer project; its proposal was written in 1955.

concepts.summary: AI studies computational methods for tasks involving reasoning, perception, language, and learning.
concepts.problem: Could machines perform activities previously associated with human intelligence?
concepts.development: The Dartmouth proposal brought diverse computational ambitions under one name. Symbolic reasoning, statistical methods, and neural approaches developed along overlapping paths.
concepts.limitations: This is a research program, not a single explanatory theory; success on tasks does not settle questions of general intelligence or consciousness.

contributors.name: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon

concepts.title: Machine learning

date.note: Samuel's checkers paper is a naming milestone; learning-machine research predates it.

concepts.summary: Programs improve task performance by adjusting from examples or experience.
concepts.problem: Explicitly writing every decision rule is difficult for complex tasks.
concepts.development: Samuel's checkers research demonstrated improvement through experience. Statistical estimation and optimization later supplied broad frameworks for generalization.
concepts.limitations: Good training performance may fail on new situations; data quality and evaluation design matter.

contributors.name: Arthur Samuel
contributors.role: Demonstrated learning in a checkers program

concepts.title: Computational complexity

date.note: Hartmanis and Stearns's paper marks a systematic resource-bounded theory.

concepts.summary: Problems are classified by the time or memory needed as input size grows.
concepts.problem: A computable problem may still be too expensive to solve.
concepts.development: Hartmanis and Stearns formalized time-bounded computation. Complexity classes made efficiency itself a mathematical object.
concepts.limitations: Worst-case growth does not fully predict practical performance; many important separations remain unproved.

concepts.title: NP-completeness

date.note: Cook's theorem is the milestone; Levin independently developed a related result.

concepts.summary: Some efficiently checkable problems are at least as hard as every problem in NP under efficient reductions.
concepts.problem: Researchers needed to recognize families of difficult search and decision problems.
concepts.development: Cook linked nondeterministic computation with logical satisfiability. Reductions subsequently connected many combinatorial problems.
concepts.limitations: NP-complete does not mean proved impossible to solve quickly; whether P equals NP remains open.

contributors.name: Richard Karp
contributors.role: Connected many combinatorial problems through reductions

concepts.title: Public-key cryptography

date.note: Diffie and Hellman's public proposal is the milestone; classified parallel discoveries were revealed later.

concepts.summary: Different but mathematically related keys permit public operations while keeping a private secret.
concepts.problem: Secure communication previously required a secret to be shared beforehand.
concepts.development: Diffie and Hellman introduced public-key ideas and key agreement, using computational difficulty as a resource.
concepts.limitations: Security depends on assumptions, parameter choices, and implementation; not every hard-looking problem is secure.

concepts.title: Distributed consensus under faults

date.note: The Byzantine generals formulation builds on earlier agreement research.

concepts.summary: Independent computers can coordinate despite some components sending inconsistent information, under specified assumptions.
concepts.problem: Replicated systems must agree even when components fail or behave maliciously.
concepts.development: Lamport, Shostak, and Pease formalized Byzantine agreement and proved bounds for communication models.
concepts.limitations: Guarantees depend on timing, authentication, and fault assumptions; they are not unconditional promises of agreement.

contributors.name: Leslie Lamport, Robert Shostak, and Marshall Pease

concepts.title: Quantum computation

date.note: Feynman's published simulation argument is a milestone; several earlier and later proposals contributed.

concepts.summary: Quantum systems process information through controlled superposition, interference, and entanglement.
concepts.problem: Simulating general quantum systems with classical resources can be costly.
concepts.development: Feynman argued for quantum simulators; later universal models and algorithms clarified computational possibilities.
concepts.limitations: Quantum computation does not accelerate every problem, and useful devices must control errors.

concepts.title: Quantum information

date.note: Schumacher's quantum-coding theorem is the milestone; the broader field has earlier roots.

concepts.summary: Quantum states have information-processing capacities that differ from ordinary classical bits.
concepts.problem: Classical coding alone does not describe compressing or transmitting unknown quantum states.
concepts.development: Schumacher connected quantum entropy to faithful compression and formalized the qubit resource. Entanglement and measurement became central operational concepts.
concepts.limitations: An unknown quantum state cannot be treated as a freely readable classical record; physical noise constrains protocols.

concepts.title: Backpropagation

date.note: Marks an influential neural-network demonstration, not the invention of reverse differentiation.

concepts.summary: The chain rule efficiently traces how each network parameter contributes to a prediction error.
concepts.problem: Multilayer networks needed practical ways to adjust hidden connections.
concepts.development: Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams popularized error backpropagation for learned representations, building on earlier differentiation and learning work.
concepts.limitations: Gradients do not guarantee a global optimum; training can be unstable or data-dependent.

contributors.name: David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams
contributors.role: Demonstrated learning hidden representations with backpropagation

concepts.title: Learning from rewards

date.note: Watkins's thesis is the Q-learning milestone; reinforcement learning has older roots.

concepts.summary: An agent improves decisions by learning from rewards accumulated over interactions.
concepts.problem: An action may have useful or harmful consequences only much later.
concepts.development: Work on dynamic programming, trial-and-error learning, and temporal differences led to methods such as Watkins's Q-learning.
concepts.limitations: Exploration can be costly, and a poorly chosen reward can produce unwanted behavior.

concepts.title: Bayesian networks

date.note: Pearl's book consolidated work developed through the preceding decade.

concepts.summary: A directed graph expresses conditional dependencies among uncertain variables.
concepts.problem: Large joint probability distributions are difficult to represent and reason with directly.
concepts.development: Pearl developed graph-based representations and local probability propagation, joining probabilistic reasoning with AI.
concepts.limitations: A dependency arrow is not automatically causal; omitted variables and incorrect independence assumptions distort inference.

contributors.name: Judea Pearl
contributors.role: Developed and synthesized probabilistic graphical reasoning

concepts.title: Graphical causal inference

date.note: The date marks Pearl's causal-diagram framework, not the beginning of causal inference as a whole.

concepts.summary: Causal diagrams make assumptions explicit and help determine which interventions can be inferred from observations.
concepts.problem: Correlation alone cannot distinguish causation from common causes or selection effects.
concepts.development: Pearl combined graphical models with intervention rules. The framework complements experimental design and other causal traditions.
concepts.limitations: The graph is an assumption, not a conclusion extracted automatically from data; unidentified effects require more information.

contributors.name: Judea Pearl
contributors.role: Developed graphical identification and intervention calculus

concepts.title: Deep representation learning

date.note: An influential deep-belief-network paper marks renewed practical progress; deep networks have older precedents.

concepts.summary: Multiple learned layers build increasingly useful representations of data.
concepts.problem: Hand-designed features often limited performance on complex perceptual tasks.
concepts.development: Hinton, Osindero, and Teh showed a practical training strategy for deep belief networks. Subsequent architectures, data, and hardware widened the approach.
concepts.limitations: Large models can overfit, inherit data biases, and fail outside their training conditions.

contributors.name: Geoffrey Hinton, Simon Osindero, and Yee-Whye Teh
contributors.role: Developed an influential deep-network training approach

concepts.title: Attention-based transformers

date.note: Publication of Attention Is All You Need.

concepts.summary: Attention lets a model combine information from different positions in a sequence according to learned relevance.
concepts.problem: Sequential processing made some language-model computations slow and long-range relationships difficult.
concepts.development: Vaswani and collaborators built an attention-centered sequence architecture. Parallel training made it influential across language and other modalities.
concepts.limitations: Attention scores are not a complete explanation of reasoning; learned patterns can reproduce errors and bias.

concepts.title: Diffusion generative models

date.note: The original nonequilibrium-thermodynamics generative proposal is the milestone.

concepts.summary: A model learns to reverse gradual corruption, turning noise into samples resembling a training distribution.
concepts.problem: Generative modeling needed flexible distributions with tractable training and sampling.
concepts.development: Sohl-Dickstein and collaborators connected diffusion processes with learned reverse dynamics. Later denoising formulations improved practical generation.
concepts.limitations: Generated samples reflect learned data patterns, not guaranteed factual or physical validity.

contributors.name: Jascha Sohl-Dickstein, Eric Weiss, Niru Maheswaranathan, and Surya Ganguli

concepts.title: Algorithmic information

date.label: c. 1964–1965
date.note: Solomonoff and Kolmogorov developed foundational formulations; Chaitin contributed independently.

concepts.summary: The shortest program producing an object provides a measure of its descriptive complexity.
concepts.problem: Shannon's average uncertainty does not directly measure the complexity of an individual string.
concepts.development: Algorithmic information joined universal computation with description length and randomness. Different universal machines change complexity only by an additive constant.
concepts.limitations: Exact shortest-description complexity is generally uncomputable; practical compressors give upper bounds.

contributors.name: Ray Solomonoff, Andrey Kolmogorov, and Gregory Chaitin
contributors.role: Developed algorithmic approaches to information and randomness

concepts.title: Formal program verification

date.note: Hoare's axiomatic paper is the milestone; Floyd and earlier work also contributed.

concepts.summary: Logical assertions describe what must hold before and after a program executes.
concepts.problem: Testing examples cannot establish every possible program behavior.
concepts.development: Hoare gave rules for proving program properties from statements and assumptions. Later tools mechanized parts of such reasoning.
concepts.limitations: A proof is only as good as its specification and modeled environment; full automation faces undecidability.

concepts.title: High-level programming languages

date.note: FORTRAN's release is the landmark; several earlier language and compiler projects existed.

concepts.summary: A compiler translates structured, human-oriented instructions into machine operations.
concepts.problem: Scientists needed to express computations without writing every hardware-level instruction.
concepts.development: Backus's IBM team developed FORTRAN and an effective compiler; Hopper and others pursued parallel paths to higher-level programming.
concepts.limitations: A convenient notation does not itself guarantee correct algorithms or safe numerical behavior.

contributors.name: John Backus and the FORTRAN team
contributors.role: Developed a practical scientific language and compiler

concepts.title: Support-vector machines

date.note: Cortes and Vapnik's soft-margin formulation generalized earlier margin classifiers.

concepts.summary: A classifier chooses a separating boundary with a large margin, allowing controlled errors.
concepts.problem: A model should separate classes while generalizing beyond its training examples.
concepts.development: Cortes and Vapnik combined margin optimization with feature-space mappings and slack variables for nonseparable data.
concepts.limitations: Performance depends on representation, kernel, and regularization choices; training can be expensive on large datasets.

concepts.title: Division of labor

date.note: Smith's Wealth of Nations is the milestone; specialized work is ancient.

concepts.summary: Dividing production into specialized tasks can increase output through practice, coordination, and tools.
concepts.problem: Political economy sought to explain differences in productivity and wealth.
concepts.development: Adam Smith illustrated how specialization and exchange alter productive capacity. Later economics examined its dependence on market scale and institutions.
concepts.limitations: Productivity gains are not automatic improvements in wellbeing; distribution, autonomy, and working conditions also matter.

concepts.title: Comparative advantage

date.note: Ricardo's published trade example is used as a landmark.

concepts.summary: Specializing according to relative opportunity costs can produce gains from exchange even without absolute superiority.
concepts.problem: Why can trade benefit two parties when one is more productive at everything?
concepts.development: Ricardo compared relative production costs, separating comparative from absolute advantage. Later models incorporated multiple factors and adjustment costs.
concepts.limitations: Aggregate gains need not reach every person; assumptions about adjustment, externalities, and institutions affect applications.
concepts.example: A person can be faster at two tasks yet gain by specializing in the one where their relative advantage is larger.

concepts.title: Marginal utility

date.note: Jevons and Menger published independently in 1871; Walras followed in the 1870s.

concepts.summary: Decisions can depend on the value of one additional unit rather than total usefulness.
concepts.problem: Economic theories needed to explain choices and exchange values at the margin.
concepts.development: Jevons applied mathematical reasoning to incremental satisfaction. Parallel marginalist traditions helped reshape theories of consumer choice.
concepts.limitations: Utility is a model of preference, not an objectively measured universal quantity of happiness.

concepts.title: Supply, demand, and equilibrium

date.note: Marshall's synthesis is the milestone, not the origin of supply and demand reasoning.

concepts.summary: A market model connects prices with quantities buyers seek and sellers offer.
concepts.problem: Economists needed to analyze how changes in conditions affect prices and exchange.
concepts.development: Marshall combined demand and cost analysis into an influential partial-equilibrium framework. The crossing of curves is a model of mutually consistent plans.
concepts.limitations: Market power, institutions, externalities, and changing expectations can invalidate simple competitive assumptions.

concepts.title: Psychophysics

date.note: Publication of Fechner's Elemente der Psychophysik.

concepts.summary: Controlled stimulus changes can be related quantitatively to reported sensations and discrimination thresholds.
concepts.problem: Could aspects of subjective experience be measured systematically?
concepts.development: Weber studied sensory discrimination; Fechner developed experimental methods and mathematical relations linking physical intensity with sensation.
concepts.limitations: Different senses and stimulus ranges require different models; a simple logarithmic law is not universal.

equation.explanation: In Fechner's model, sensation S grows logarithmically with intensity I relative to a reference I₀; k sets the scale. Its range of validity is limited.

concepts.title: Experimental psychology

date.note: Wundt's Leipzig laboratory is an institutional milestone; experimental mental science had earlier roots.

concepts.summary: Questions about perception, attention, and mental processes can be investigated with controlled experiments.
concepts.problem: Speculation about the mind needed repeatable observations and measurements.
concepts.development: Wundt organized laboratory research, drawing on physiology and psychophysics. Later approaches broadened participants, tasks, and methods.
concepts.limitations: Early introspective methods were limited; experiments require careful operational definitions and appropriate populations.

contributors.name: William James
contributors.role: Developed a major alternative account of mental function

concepts.title: Classical conditioning

date.label: c. 1903
date.note: Pavlov reported conditioned-reflex work around this period; experiments developed across several years.

concepts.summary: An organism can learn that one stimulus predicts another and respond in anticipation.
concepts.problem: Digestive experiments revealed responses occurring before food arrived.
concepts.development: Pavlov measured salivation and manipulated stimulus pairings. Conditioning became a controlled framework for studying associative learning.
concepts.limitations: Learning depends on predictiveness and biological constraints; simple stimulus pairing does not explain all learning.

concepts.title: Behaviorism

date.note: Publication of Watson's behaviorist manifesto.

concepts.summary: Behaviorism emphasized observable behavior and environmental relations as psychology's scientific subject matter.
concepts.problem: Introspection raised concerns about subjectivity and reproducibility.
concepts.development: Watson advocated an objective behavioral science. Learning experiments expanded the approach; later cognitive theories challenged its exclusion of internal representations.
concepts.limitations: Behavioral methods remain valuable, but a strict rejection of internal processes is not a complete account of mind.

concepts.title: Gestalt principles of perception

date.note: Wertheimer's apparent-motion work began in 1912; the cited organization paper appeared in 1923.

concepts.summary: Perception organizes stimuli into structured wholes, influenced by proximity, similarity, and continuity.
concepts.problem: Collections of sensory elements did not explain the coherent objects people perceive.
concepts.development: Wertheimer, Köhler, and Koffka studied organization and apparent motion. Their principles shaped perceptual research and later design practice.
concepts.limitations: Grouping principles describe robust tendencies but do not constitute a complete neural mechanism or universal rule.

contributors.name: Max Wertheimer
contributors.role: Studied apparent motion and perceptual organization

concepts.title: Operant conditioning

date.note: Skinner's The Behavior of Organisms consolidated the experimental program.

concepts.summary: Consequences alter how likely an action is to occur again.
concepts.problem: Learning involves actions that change the environment, not just reflexes to stimuli.
concepts.development: Thorndike's law of effect preceded Skinner's controlled studies of reinforcement schedules and behavior. The approach made consequences experimentally manipulable.
concepts.limitations: Reinforcement is context-dependent; it does not remove the roles of cognition, biology, and social learning.

concepts.title: Information-processing psychology

date.label: c. 1956
date.note: A mid-century milestone, not a single founding event; Miller's paper provides a concrete example.

concepts.summary: Mental processes can be modeled as transformations of information constrained by attention and memory.
concepts.problem: Behavior alone did not explain the organization and limits of complex thought.
concepts.development: Miller used information theory to study judgment and memory capacity. Broader cognitive research developed testable models of internal representations.
concepts.limitations: Computer analogies are models, not evidence that every mental process works like a digital computer.

contributors.name: Jerome Bruner and other cognitive researchers
contributors.role: Developed experimental accounts of internal processing

concepts.title: Working memory

date.note: Publication of Baddeley and Hitch's working-memory account.

concepts.summary: A limited-capacity system temporarily maintains and manipulates information during thought.
concepts.problem: A passive short-term store did not adequately explain concurrent memory and reasoning tasks.
concepts.development: Baddeley and Hitch used dual-task evidence to propose interacting storage and control components. Later models refined their organization.
concepts.limitations: Competing accounts differ over the nature of capacity and control; component labels are not literal brain compartments.

concepts.title: Observational learning

date.note: The Bobo-doll study is a milestone; observational learning research predates it.

concepts.summary: People can acquire behavior by watching others, without directly receiving the same rewards.
concepts.problem: Learning theories needed to explain imitation and the influence of social models.
concepts.development: Bandura, Dorothea Ross, and Sheila Ross experimentally studied children's imitation. Later social-cognitive theories added expectations and self-regulation.
concepts.limitations: A laboratory imitation task does not by itself establish durable real-world behavior; context and ethics matter.

contributors.name: Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross, and Sheila Ross

concepts.title: Cognitive dissonance

date.note: Festinger's theory preceded the 1959 forced-compliance experiment.

concepts.summary: Inconsistency between beliefs and actions can motivate changes that reduce psychological discomfort.
concepts.problem: People sometimes change attitudes after acting against them.
concepts.development: Festinger proposed the theory; experiments with Carlsmith explored how justification affects attitude change. Subsequent research tested competing explanations and boundary conditions.
concepts.limitations: The theory is not a universal explanation for disagreement; self-perception and other mechanisms can produce similar observations.

concepts.title: Mathematical game theory

date.note: Von Neumann and Morgenstern's book is the synthesis milestone; earlier strategic mathematics existed.

concepts.summary: Outcomes depend on the choices of multiple agents whose interests may align or conflict.
concepts.problem: Ordinary optimization omits the fact that other decision-makers also adapt.
concepts.development: Von Neumann's strategic mathematics and Morgenstern's economics formed a shared framework of players, strategies, and payoffs.
concepts.limitations: A mathematically valid solution concept does not guarantee that real people know the game or behave as assumed.

contributors.name: John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern

concepts.title: Nash equilibrium

date.note: Nash announced an existence result in 1950 and developed it further in 1951.

concepts.summary: A strategy profile is an equilibrium when no player benefits by changing their own strategy alone.
concepts.problem: Game theory needed a general solution concept beyond two-player zero-sum games.
concepts.development: Nash used fixed-point reasoning to prove mixed-strategy equilibrium existence for finite games.
concepts.limitations: An equilibrium need not be fair, unique, efficient, easy to find, or a realistic prediction.

contributors.name: John Nash
contributors.role: Defined the equilibrium concept and proved an existence theorem

concepts.example: An equilibrium may leave everyone worse off than cooperation; stability and collective benefit are different properties.

concepts.title: Expected utility

date.note: Marks axiomatic expected utility; Bernoulli's risk analysis dates to 1738.

concepts.summary: Uncertain options can be ranked by probability-weighted utility when preferences satisfy specified consistency conditions.
concepts.problem: Expected money alone fails to capture risk-sensitive choices.
concepts.development: Von Neumann and Morgenstern formalized utility over lotteries, building on earlier risk reasoning. The framework became central to decision analysis.
concepts.limitations: It is a normative model under assumptions; observed choices often violate those assumptions.

contributors.name: John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern
Daniel Bernoulli
contributors.role: Developed an earlier utility account of risk

equation.explanation: Expected utility sums each outcome's utility u(xᵢ), weighted by its probability pᵢ.

concepts.title: Prospect theory

date.note: Publication of Kahneman and Tversky's original model.

concepts.summary: Choices under risk depend on reference points, perceived gains and losses, and nonlinear probability weighting.
concepts.problem: Observed decisions systematically departed from standard expected-utility predictions.
concepts.development: Kahneman and Tversky built a descriptive model from choice experiments, connecting psychophysics with economic decision-making.
concepts.limitations: Predictions depend on reference points and context; the model is not a universal account of every decision.

concepts.title: Behavioral economics

date.note: Thaler's consumer-choice paper is a milestone; psychological economics has a longer history.

concepts.summary: Economic models can incorporate measured limits of attention, self-control, and social preferences.
concepts.problem: Idealized rational-choice models left systematic patterns in behavior unexplained.
concepts.development: Thaler connected psychological evidence with consumer theory. Experiments and formal models developed testable accounts of departures from standard assumptions.
concepts.limitations: Effects vary across populations and institutions; identifying a bias does not alone establish the best policy.

concepts.title: Randomized field experiments

date.label: c. 1995
date.note: Marks influential development-economics experiments; randomized social research is much older.

concepts.summary: Random allocation of an intervention helps compare outcomes without systematic initial treatment selection.
concepts.problem: Policy correlations often mix intervention effects with preexisting differences.
concepts.development: Kremer's education studies and later work by Banerjee, Duflo, and collaborators adapted randomized trials to development questions.
concepts.limitations: Attrition, spillovers, ethics, and generalization require care; a local effect is not a universal policy result.

contributors.name: Michael Kremer
contributors.role: Conducted influential early development field experiments

relationships.explanation: Counting repetitions is a conceptual prerequisite for comparing days, lunar months, and seasonal cycles.
Long-term positional observations supplied phenomena for mathematical Earth-centered models to explain.
Circles and angular geometry supplied the mathematical language of epicycles.
Copernicus reorganized inherited planetary models by placing Earth in motion around the Sun.
Kepler investigated planetary motions within a Sun-centered arrangement and replaced circular paths with ellipses.
Ellipse geometry and areas express the first two laws; this link identifies mathematical dependence.
Precise telescopic angular measurements made annual stellar displacement detectable.
Earth's orbital baseline gives annual parallax its geometric interpretation.
Triangulation converts a baseline and small angle into a stellar distance.
Stellar absorption spectra supplied the features used to classify stars.
Repeated photographic observations of faint stars enabled Leavitt to compare pulsation periods and brightness.
Spectral categories supplied a temperature-related axis for comparing luminosities.
Distance measurements allowed apparent brightness to be converted into intrinsic luminosity.
Relativistic cosmological solutions allowed the overall scale of the universe to evolve.
Cepheid distances helped establish the relation between galaxy distances and recession measurements.
Galaxy spectra provided redshifts used in establishing expansion.
Running an expanding universe backward motivated a denser earlier state.
Relativistic dynamics provide the mathematical framework for evolving-universe models.
Mass–energy equivalence connects the nuclear mass difference with released energy.
Quantum nuclear behavior is needed to calculate reactions in stellar interiors.
Stellar energy-producing reactions became part of a broader account of element formation.
Measured elemental abundances constrain proposed nuclear production pathways.
Electron degeneracy is a quantum effect supporting a dense remnant.
Relativistic electron behavior is central to the limiting-mass argument.
Compact-remnant physics raised the question of stellar endpoints beyond electron-supported configurations.
Schwarzschild's solution follows from Einstein's gravitational field equations.
A hot early universe predicted relic radiation that could be sought observationally.
Sensitive microwave receivers allowed the faint all-sky background to be detected.
Dynamical estimates compare observed velocities with the gravity expected from visible mass.
Inflation was proposed to address initial-condition puzzles left by the standard hot-universe model.
Inflationary scenarios often use field dynamics and vacuum-like energy in an expanding spacetime.
The uniformity and fluctuation pattern of the background constrain inflationary explanations.
Supernova distances showed that late expansion accelerates rather than following a matter-only decelerating history.
Relativistic cosmology relates the expansion rate to matter, pressure, and a possible cosmological constant.
Orbital periods and motions connect detected timing or velocity changes with planetary systems.
Precise Doppler measurements can reveal a star's motion caused by an orbiting planet.
Relativity predicts deflection of light in a curved spacetime.
Comparing stellar positions near the eclipsed Sun enabled an early light-deflection test.
Relativity predicts traveling spacetime disturbances and their measurable effect on distance.
Models of merging black holes supplied signals against which detector data could be compared.
Radio waves are electromagnetic radiation, extending astronomy beyond visible wavelengths.
The distance–redshift relation supplied an approximate depth axis for galaxy surveys.
Gravitational clustering of unseen matter provides a framework for explaining the observed cosmic web.
The concordance model retains the hot, expanding early-universe framework.
Precision microwave measurements constrain the model's parameters.
A cold dark-matter component accounts for gravitational observations and structure growth in the model.
A cosmological constant provides the model's simplest account of accelerated expansion.
Counter movements implement arithmetic procedures on represented quantities.
Place value explains how columns or positions can stand for different magnitudes; this is a conceptual comparison.
Gears embody addition and positional carrying as repeatable operations.
Babbage generalized mechanical calculation toward a programmable engine with separate store and mill.
A programmable engine requires a sequence of executable numerical instructions.
The machine model formalizes the idea of effective step-by-step calculation.
Questions about mechanical logical decision motivated Turing's investigation.
Church developed function abstraction in a foundational logical setting.
A precise universal machine model makes the undecidability argument possible.
Logical combinations can be realized by idealized threshold units.
McCulloch and Pitts explicitly analyzed idealized neural activity with propositional logic.
Universal computation explains how encoded instructions can specify many different procedures; this is a conceptual link.
Binary encoding provides a common representation for instructions and data in many stored-program machines.
Shannon's uncertainty measure and channel models are defined using probabilities.
Logarithms turn multiplicative numbers of possibilities into additive information quantities.
Information and noisy communication form a shared mathematical language for feedback; this is a conceptual connection between contemporary works.
Continuous feedback dynamics can be modeled using rates of change.
Reliable transmission in noise provides the mathematical problem that error-correcting codes address.
Parity constraints operate on binary values to distinguish valid codewords.
General computation provides a framework for implementing reasoning procedures.
The Dartmouth proposal explicitly included neural nets among its research directions.
Learning through experience became one of the practical approaches pursued within AI.
Statistical inference supplies a conceptual basis for estimating patterns from finite examples.
Resource limits refine an abstract model of computation into time and space classes.
Polynomial-time bounds and reductions make completeness a precise statement.
Boolean satisfiability provides a central complete decision problem.
The public-key approach distinguishes feasible operations from computations intended to be infeasible.
Diffie and Hellman explicitly connected cryptographic problems with communication and computation theory.
Agreement protocols specify precise local rules for messages and decisions.
Correctness arguments establish agreement guarantees under an explicit fault model.
Controlled quantum evolution supplies operations unavailable in an ordinary classical model.
Feynman's discussion asks how physical simulation relates to universal computation.
Schumacher's coding theorem is explicitly analogous to Shannon's classical noiseless coding theorem.
Quantum states, measurements, and density operators define the information being encoded.
Entangled states have joint properties central to quantum coding and communication.
Multilayer networks supplied the learnable parameters and hidden representations addressed by the method.
The chain rule propagates output derivatives through intermediate computations.
Computed gradients provide directions for adjusting parameters to reduce a loss.
Trial-and-error experience supplies data for learning improved decisions.
Reward-based learning provides a conceptual bridge between behavioral learning and computational agents, without equating the two.
Stochastic environments and expected returns require probabilistic reasoning.
Conditional probabilities update beliefs as observations arrive.
Directed graphs encode dependency structure and guide inference algorithms.
Causal diagrams extend graphical probabilistic reasoning with assumptions about interventions.
Identification relates causal assumptions to quantities estimated from observed distributions.
Deep models extend neural computation through multiple representation layers.
Gradient-based fine-tuning adjusts layers after initialization or pretraining.
Deep networks learn useful representations from data rather than requiring all features to be specified manually.
Transformers are learned multilayer architectures for representing and transforming sequences.
Matrix operations implement projections and attention-weighted combinations.
Neural networks parameterize the learned reverse process.
The original diffusion-model proposal explicitly draws inspiration from nonequilibrium thermodynamics.
Forward and reverse stochastic processes describe distributions over data.
A universal description language supplies the programs whose shortest lengths define complexity.
Algorithmic approaches address information in individual descriptions, complementing average probabilistic entropy.
Axioms and inference rules establish program properties deductively.
Undecidability explains why unrestricted program correctness cannot be automated completely.
Programmable machines can execute translated code produced by a compiler.
FORTRAN allowed scientists to express numerical formulas in a higher-level notation.
Support-vector methods address learning classification rules from examples.
The margin and slack-variable formulation defines a constrained optimization problem.
Vectors, inner products, and hyperplanes express the separating boundary.
Comparing output per worker uses quantitative production measures; this is an editorial prerequisite link.
The specialization-and-exchange problem expands from tasks within production to relative costs across trading partners.
Ratios of required inputs express opportunity costs in Ricardo's numerical example.
Marginal analysis uses incremental changes and, in mathematical formulations, derivatives.
Marshall integrated marginal demand reasoning with production-cost analysis.
Systematic stimulus and response measurements make sensory comparisons quantitative.
Fechner explicitly related differential and integral formulas in sensory measurement.
Quantitative sensory experiments helped establish laboratory methods for studying the mind.
Controlled manipulation and repeatable observations make mental processes investigable.
Manipulating stimulus pairings makes competing accounts of anticipatory responses testable.
Conditioned-response research supported a focus on measurable relations between environment and behavior.
Watson redirected the experimental program away from introspection toward observable behavior.
Gestalt research challenged accounts that reduced perception to isolated sensory elements.
Skinner developed an experimentally controlled behavioral program centered on consequences.
Operant conditioning distinguishes learning through action consequences from learning stimulus predictions.
Miller explicitly used information theory to analyze limits of judgment and memory.
Cognitive models reintroduced internal information-processing mechanisms into experimental explanation.
Working-memory models explain the temporary storage and manipulation needed for ongoing thought.
Observational learning showed how acquiring behavior could be studied without each learner receiving direct reinforcement.
Controlled attitude-change experiments tested predictions of cognitive inconsistency.
Mixed strategies and uncertain outcomes require probabilities over actions and results.
Utility over uncertain outcomes supplies payoffs for strategic analysis; the two were developed together in the 1944 synthesis.
Nash generalized strategic equilibrium beyond the earlier zero-sum setting.
Expected utility weights each possible outcome's utility by its probability.
Preference-based utility provides a conceptual bridge from consumption choices to choices over uncertain outcomes.
Prospect theory modeled systematic departures from expected-utility predictions in risky choices.
Kahneman described nonlinear psychological responses as central to the development of the theory.
Reference dependence and related experimental findings informed psychologically realistic economic models.
Behavioral consumer models challenge and extend assumptions used in standard demand analysis.
Random assignment and comparison groups were adapted to interventions in social and economic settings.
Statistical estimation quantifies treatment differences and their uncertainty.
